name: welcome
text: Hello! Every program leans on the operating system's kernel: to print, to read a file, to start another program. kSEE lets you watch the kernel, Linux, do that work, one step at a time, right here in your browser.

The program below asks the kernel two things. `int fd = dup(1)` gets a second number, `fd`, for the screen (number 1); `write(fd, "hello\n", 6)` prints hello through it. Each such request is a syscall, and the kernel's answer is at the end of its line.

The kernel kept a record of everything it did. Follow [the write](vfs_write) into the kernel, the part every file's write goes through, then step with the arrow keys; what it printed is in the [Console](console) tab.

Now make it yours: click a line and change it; it runs again as you press Enter or click away. Or try one ready made: [print something else](try:1); [a number that is not open](try:2): the kernel refuses, -9, EBADF; [a pointer that is not the program's](try:3): -14, EFAULT, the kernel checks before it reads; or [a number closed first](try:4).
title: Welcome to kSEE

name: start
text: A process names the files it has open by small numbers, file descriptors: 0, 1 and 2 are open from the start, and 1 is the console. `int fd = dup(1)` asks for one more number for the same file, and the kernel answers with the lowest number not in use: 3.

And it remembers: from now on, 3 is the console too, for this process, until it is closed. What the kernel remembers is its state; syscalls are how a program reads and changes it. The kernel's own function for dup is [__wasm_sys_dup](__wasm_sys_dup); the next lessons show how to read what it did.
Try: [dup twice](try:1): 3, then 4; or [close 2 first](try:2): then dup answers 2, the lowest free number again.
title: Why 3? A syscall changes the kernel

name: timeline
text: The program now makes two calls: `dup(1)`, then `close(fd)`, which gives the number back. Click a line of the program to select its call.

Above the source is the timeline of the call selected, time going left to right. Each bar is a function the kernel ran, as wide as the lines it ran; a function sits on the one that called it. So the bottom row is the way in for every syscall, [wasm_syscall](wasm_syscall); above it is the syscall's own function, [__wasm_sys_dup](__wasm_sys_dup); above that, what it called, as [alloc_fd](alloc_fd), finding the free number.

The colors say which part of the kernel a function is from: files green (`fs/`), the core kernel warm (`kernel/`, and `mm/`, memory), the machine blue (`arch/`, `drivers/`), helpers gray (`lib/`, `include/`).

Move the pointer over the timeline: the whole page shows that moment, the source at the line running then, the Stack on the right with the calls that led there. Click to keep it there; then the arrow keys move it, as the next lesson shows. The wheel zooms (up and down) and pans (sideways); a drag pans too.

The thin strip on top is the whole recording: where each call begins, and between them, the other tasks the kernel ran (the strip under the timeline names the task running: `prog`, the program, or one of the kernel's own, as `swapper`, the idle task). [The second call](__wasm_sys_close) undoes the first: 3 is free again.
title: Reading the timeline

name: stepping
text: The cursor is a moment of the recording: the source shows the line running then, marked, and the Stack the calls that led there, the innermost on top, each with its arguments and local variables as they were then. Move it with the buttons under the timeline, or the arrow keys:

→ Next goes through the function you are reading, a line at a time, over the calls it makes. ↑ In goes into the call the line makes (with none, on to the next line: ↑ alone follows every line the kernel ran). ← Back goes back in time the way you came, through the function after →, every line after ↑. ↓ Out goes back to the caller, at its call.

1. Start at [vfs_write](vfs_write), the layer every file's write goes through, and step with →. Before it writes anything, it checks: is the file open for writing (its `f_mode` has `FMODE_WRITE`), can it be written at all, and is the buffer the program's to read (`access_ok`)? Each check is a line that ran; one that failed would return its error there.
2. [rw_verify_area](rw_verify_area) checks the position and the size: → steps over it, its answer 0, nothing wrong; ↑ on its line goes in instead, and ↓ comes back out.

3. Then the write itself, `file->f_op->write`: the file's own write, the console's. ↑ on that line goes into [console_dev_write](console_dev_write), which hands the 6 bytes to the page; ↓ back out, and →: `vfs_write` returns 6, the bytes written, as the program's line says.
On the Stack, `file`, `buf` and `count` are vfs_write's arguments, as they were then: click `file` to open its `struct file`, with `f_mode` and `f_op`.
title: Stepping through a syscall

name: changes
text: The [Memory](wasm_syscall/memory) tab lists what the call you read wrote in the kernel's memory, with what it called: here the whole syscall, from its way in, `wasm_syscall` (the call at the bottom of the Stack; ↑ and ↓ narrow and widen it). Each object it changed, what it is, and each member with its value before and after.

1. The process's table of open files, its `struct files_struct` (`current->files`): `fd_array[3]` from NULL to the console's `struct file`; `open_fds_init[0]` from 7 to 15, in binary 0111 to 1111, bit 3 now set too; and `next_fd`, where the next search starts, 4.
2. The console's `struct file` counts one more reference, `f_ref`: two numbers now stand for it, and it stays open until both are closed.
3. The program's own `task_struct`: `regs`, where the way in, `wasm_syscall`, keeps the call's number (23, dup's), its arguments, and its result, 3.

Click a row to go there: just after that write, the line that made it in the source. The [Tasks](fd_install/tasks) tab lists every task the kernel has, at the cursor: the program, `prog`, running; the kernel's own threads asleep or waiting their turn. Open one for its `task_struct`, the kernel's record of it: its `files` is the table dup changed.
Try: [close it again](try:1): `close(fd)` sets each back.
title: What a call changed

name: layers
text: A kernel is built in layers, each hiding the one below from the one above. Printing is a write to a file, `write(fd, "hello\n", 6)`, and it goes down through each layer; on the timeline, they are stacked: [the write](ksys_write).
1. The syscall: [ksys_write](ksys_write) turns the number 3 into the open file it stands for, a `struct file`, through the table dup filled, and the position to write at.

2. The VFS, [vfs_write](vfs_write), the layer that is the same for every kind of file: is the file open for writing, is the buffer readable? On the Stack: `count` is 6, the bytes of "hello" and a newline.
3. The driver, [console_dev_write](console_dev_write): the file's own write, the console's.

4. Below the driver there would be hardware. This kernel runs in a browser, so its machine is the page: the driver hands the bytes to it, and it shows them in the [Console](console) tab. The disk, later on, is the same: an image the page keeps.

Try: [fd 1 instead](try:1), the same file: the same layers; or [fd 5](try:2), not open: the call stops at the first layer and returns -9, EBADF, a failed call's result being its error's number, negative.
title: From a line to the screen: the kernel's layers

name: getpid
text: The same way in as dup, a different question. `getpid()` has no arguments and one number back, but the number is not simply stored in the task: a process's id is a `struct pid`, with a number for each pid namespace it is seen from.
1. getpid returns the id of the task's thread group, not of the task itself: [task_tgid_vnr](task_tgid_vnr) asks for `current`'s, the task running, as its caller sees it.

2. [__task_pid_nr_ns](__task_pid_nr_ns) takes two things: the `struct pid` of the thread group (`task_pid_ptr`: in `current->signal`, shared by the process's threads), and the pid namespace the caller is in (`task_active_pid_ns`).

3. [pid_nr_ns](pid_nr_ns) reads the number: a `struct pid` has one per namespace level, and here there is one level, so it is `numbers[0].nr`: the program's pid (/init, the first process, is 1; the kernel's own threads, and then the program, come after it).
Try: [from a thread](try:1): a thread of the program gets the same getpid (its thread group's), but its own gettid.
title: Which process am I? getpid()
tries: void *mem = mmap2(NULL, 65536, PROT_READ | PROT_WRITE, MAP_PRIVATE | MAP_ANONYMOUS, -1, 0)
pid_t thread = clone(CLONE_VM | CLONE_FS | CLONE_FILES | CLONE_SIGHAND | CLONE_THREAD | CLONE_SYSVSEM, mem + 65536, NULL, NULL, 0)

name: prctl
text: getpid read a task's field; prctl can write one. A task's name is `comm`, 16 bytes in its `task_struct`: what ps and top show, and the timeline here. The program renames itself.
1. [__wasm_sys_prctl](__wasm_sys_prctl) is one big switch on the option, `PR_SET_NAME` here; first [cap_task_prctl](cap_task_prctl), the security module, gets a say.
2. [strncpy_from_user](strncpy_from_user) copies the new name in from the program's memory, at most 15 bytes and a NUL: the kernel never uses a user pointer as it is.
3. [__set_task_comm](__set_task_comm) copies it into `comm`, under the task's lock, padded with zeros: [what it changed](__set_task_comm/memory), `comm` from "prog" to "worker".
The Tasks tab lists every task of the kernel, what each is doing, and its `task_struct`: open the program's, and step: `comm` changes at the call.
Try: [read it back](try:1), with `PR_GET_NAME`, into a buffer of the program's; or [a name too long](try:2): it is cut to 15 characters.
title: How does a task get its name?

name: exec
text: prctl renamed the task; running a program names it too, after the program. `execve` replaces the program a process runs: the task stays, with its pid; its memory and its program are new.
1. [do_execveat_common](do_execveat_common) opens the file ([do_open_execat](do_open_execat)), and [load_wasm_binary](load_wasm_binary), this kernel's loader for wasm programs, reads it in.

2. [begin_new_exec](begin_new_exec) is the point of no return: [exec_mmap](exec_mmap) gives the task new memory (a new `mm_struct`; the old one goes), its signal handlers are reset ([flush_signal_handlers](flush_signal_handlers)), and [__set_task_comm](__set_task_comm) names it after the program. [What it changed](begin_new_exec/memory).

3. The call does not return: the new program runs, from its start. Here it is /bin/prog again, the page's program, so it takes the next call, getpid: the same pid as before ([__task_pid_nr_ns](getpid/__task_pid_nr_ns)).
title: Running a program

name: thread
program: void *mem = mmap2(NULL, 65536, PROT_READ | PROT_WRITE, MAP_PRIVATE | MAP_ANONYMOUS, -1, 0)
pid_t thread = clone(CLONE_VM | CLONE_FS | CLONE_FILES | CLONE_SIGHAND | CLONE_THREAD | CLONE_SYSVSEM, mem + 65536, NULL, NULL, 0)
text: A process so far had one task. A thread is another task in the same process: it shares the memory, the files, the name space, and has a stack of its own.
1. The stack first: [do_mmap](do_mmap) gives the program 64 KiB of anonymous, zeroed memory for it (no MMU here, so at one address, the same for every thread).

2. [copy_process](copy_process) makes the new task. The CLONE_ flags say what it shares instead of copies: memory (CLONE_VM), files, the file system's state, signal handlers, and the thread group (CLONE_THREAD): that makes it a thread, not a child. [wake_up_new_task](wake_up_new_task) puts it on the run queue; it starts at the top of its stack, `mem + 65536` (stacks grow down).

3. The thread asks who it is: getpid gives the process's id, the same as the program's (the thread group's), but gettid its own: [__task_pid_nr_ns](gettid/__task_pid_nr_ns) with the task's own pid, not the group's.
Its calls have their own task column, headed by the thread's name, and the Tasks tab lists it with the program.
Try: [a child instead](try:1): without CLONE_THREAD and the others, a process of its own (but for CLONE_VM, sharing memory: there is no MMU to give it its own), with its own getpid.
title: How is a thread made?
tries: void *mem = mmap2(NULL, 65536, PROT_READ | PROT_WRITE, MAP_PRIVATE | MAP_ANONYMOUS, -1, 0)
pid_t child = clone(CLONE_VM | SIGCHLD, mem + 65536, NULL, NULL, 0)

name: open-close
text: fd 1 was open already. The others a program gets from open(), and gives back with close(). In the kernel the number is an index into the process's table of open files, and what it points to is a `struct file`.
1. [get_unused_fd_flags](get_unused_fd_flags) takes the lowest free slot of the table. 0, 1 and 2 are taken (the console), so the answer will be 3.
2. [path_openat](path_openat) finds the file by its path, one name at a time from the root: "note.txt" in /, an in-memory file system (ramfs).
3. [do_dentry_open](do_dentry_open) makes the open file itself, a `struct file`: which inode, where the program is in it (its position, 0), and how it was opened (read only).
4. [fd_install](fd_install) puts that struct file into slot 3, and the call returns 3.
Closing undoes it in the other order: [file_close_fd](file_close_fd) empties slot 3, so the number is free again, and [__fput](__fput) frees the struct file, which nothing refers to any more.
Try: [open the same file twice](try:1) before closing, and see what number the second open gets; or [close it twice](try:2): the second close fails with EBADF, decided before any file is looked at.
title: What is a file descriptor?

name: dup
text: An fd is only a number; behind it is the open file, a `struct file`. Two fds can stand for the same one: `dup`.

1. [fget_raw](fget_raw) finds the open file fd 3 stands for, and counts one more reference to it; [get_unused_fd_flags](dup/get_unused_fd_flags) takes the lowest free slot, 4; [fd_install](dup/fd_install) puts the same `struct file` there. [What it changed](dup/fd_install/memory): `fd_array[4]`, the same file as `fd_array[3]`.
2. The position is the open file's, not the fd's: the read through fd moves `f_pos` from 0 to 5 ("hello"), and [the read through fd2](read#2/ksys_read) goes on from 5 (" from"): see `buf`.
Try: [open it twice instead](try:1): two opens make two open files, each with its own position, so the second read starts at 0 again.
title: Two fds, one file

name: read
text: With the file open, reading from it. The bytes go through three layers, and here the file is in memory, so no disk is involved.
1. [ksys_read](ksys_read) is the syscall's entry: the fd turns into the open file (a `struct file`) and the position to read at, which starts at 0.
2. [vfs_read](vfs_read) is the VFS, the same for every file system: is the file open for reading, is the range sane, then it calls the file system's own read.

3. [filemap_read](filemap_read) is the page cache: a file's data lives in memory pages. Find the page at the position, copy from it to the program's buffer. In ramfs the pages are all the file is, so this is where the bytes come from.

[What it stored](ksys_read/memory): the file's position, the count read. [What filemap_read changed](filemap_read/memory): the page's flags (it has been read: referenced), the inode's access time, the file's read-ahead state; and the page is the inode's (its `mapping`). The position it read at, and moved on, is the `kiocb`'s `ki_pos` (0 to 18), a local of `new_sync_read`'s: the Stack shows it, with `count` and `buf`. Try: [read twice](try:1): the position has moved, so the second read returns 0, the end of the file; or [4 bytes at a time](try:2).
To find any function in the recording: type part of its name in the box above the timeline, `copy`, say: its bars light up, and Enter goes to the next call.
title: What happens in read()?

name: write
text: Now the other way, into the file: the program appends a line. Where do the bytes go?
1. [ksys_write](ksys_write) turns the fd into the open file; with O_APPEND, the position is the file's end, not the file's position.
2. [generic_perform_write](generic_perform_write) copies the bytes from the program into the file's pages in the page cache. In ramfs that is where the file is, so this is the whole write.
3. [simple_write_end](simple_write_end) makes the file 5 bytes longer: its inode's size grows.

Try: [without O_APPEND](try:1) the write overwrites the file's start, the position being 0. [A write of 4000 bytes](try:2) (zeros), appended after what is there, crosses a page boundary, so the loop in `generic_perform_write` runs twice.
title: What does write() do?

name: open-fails
text: Every open so far worked. Here two fail, and each error is decided in a different place: a name that is not there, and a directory opened for writing.

1. [path_openat](path_openat) walks the path one name at a time from the root. "missing" is not in the dentry cache (the kernel's memory of names), and an in-memory file system has nowhere else to look: [simple_lookup](simple_lookup) says no such file, and the call returns ENOENT.
2. In the second call the name is found, but [do_open](do_open) sees a directory opened for writing: EISDIR.
Try: [add O_CREAT to the first call](try:1): now the missing name is made, and the same path takes a different branch.
title: Why does open() fail?

name: create
text: A missing name fails an open, unless the open asks for it to be made: O_CREAT. What does the kernel make?

The path walk reaches "new.txt" and finds no such name; with O_CREAT, [lookup_open](lookup_open) asks the file system to make it. In ramfs, [ramfs_mknod](ramfs_mknod) makes two things: a new inode, which is the file itself (its mode, its size, its pages), and a name for it in the directory, a dentry pointing at that inode.
Then the open goes on as any open: a `struct file`, a slot in the fd table, and the call returns the fd. [The objects it made and changed](wasm_syscall/memory) are on the right.

Try: [create the same file twice](try:1): the second time the name is there, so `lookup_open` takes the other branch and nothing is made. [With O_EXCL](try:2) the second open fails with EEXIST instead.
title: How is a file made?

name: dir
text: The names files have live in directories: a directory is names, each pointing to a file. Here one is made and the root is listed, all in memory.
1. [ramfs_mkdir](ramfs_mkdir) makes the new directory: an inode like a file's, and a name for it, "sub", in /.

2. Listing / with getdents64: in an in-memory file system the directory's names are the dentry cache itself, so [dcache_readdir](dcache_readdir) walks the children of /, and for each [filldir64](filldir64) copies an entry out to the program: its name, its inode number, its type. The program's line shows the names it got.
Try: [make the directory twice](try:1): the second mkdirat fails with EEXIST. Or [list the new directory itself](try:2): it has only "." and "..".
title: What is a directory?

name: ext4-read
text: So far every file was in memory. Now a disk: the same read, of a file on ext4 (on a disk). Where do the bytes come from the first time?
1. Opening it: the name is not in the dentry cache yet, so [ext4_lookup](ext4_lookup) reads the directory's block from the disk to find it.
Try: [read twice](try:1): the page is in the cache after the first read, so the second has no block layer and no ext4 read path in it: the timeline shows it much shorter.
title: Reading from a disk

name: ext4-create
text: The same create as in memory, but on ext4. A disk file system has to keep track of what it used, so that it is still right after a crash.
1. [ext4_create](ext4_create) makes the file, all inside one journal transaction, so that a crash leaves all of it or none of it.
2. [__ext4_new_inode](__ext4_new_inode) finds a free inode in a block group's inode bitmap and marks it used.
3. [add_dirent_to_buf](add_dirent_to_buf) writes the name "new.txt" into free space in a block of the directory, next to the other names.

Try: [a file in a directory that does not exist](try:1): the lookup fails before ext4_create ever runs. Compare [ext4_create](ext4_create) with the in-memory create's `ramfs_mknod`: how much more a disk file system does.
title: Making a file on a disk

name: ext4-write
text: The same write as in memory, but on ext4. Is anything written to the disk?

[ext4_buffered_write_iter](ext4_buffered_write_iter) puts the bytes into the page cache, as in memory, and marks the page dirty: to be written back later. [ext4_da_write_begin](ext4_da_write_begin) is delayed allocation: no disk block is chosen for the data yet, one is only reserved. So nothing reaches the disk in this call; that happens in writeback, or in fsync (the next example).
Try: [open with O_SYNC](try:1): the write itself then has to reach the disk, and the run grows by the whole writeback path.
title: Writing to a file on a disk
tries: int fd = openat(AT_FDCWD, "/mnt/new.txt", O_CREAT | O_WRONLY | O_SYNC, 0644)

name: durable
text: The last write left the bytes in memory, to be written back later. fsync() asks for them to be durable now. What does that take?

1. [ext4_sync_file](ext4_sync_file): the data must reach the disk. The dirty page is written back, and now [ext4_mb_new_blocks](ext4_mb_new_blocks), the multiblock allocator, chooses a block for it from the block bitmap.

2. The metadata changes (the bitmaps, the inode, the directory block) go through the journal: [jbd2_journal_commit_transaction](jbd2_journal_commit_transaction) commits them, on jbd2's own thread. Look at the task strip in the timeline: the CPU changes hands.

3. Every request to the disk goes through the block layer: [submit_bio](fsync/submit_bio) sends one to the disk, /dev/wda: its driver, [wasm_disk_queue_rq](fsync/wasm_disk_queue_rq), hands it to the disk and returns, the task waits, and the disk's interrupt ends it.
Try: [without the fsync](try:1), the write and the close leave everything in memory. [With two fsyncs](try:2), the second has nothing dirty to write and returns almost at once.
title: How does a write reach the disk?

name: ext4-dir
text: The same mkdir as in memory, but on ext4, where a directory is a file of names in disk blocks.

1. [ext4_mkdir](ext4_mkdir) makes the directory in one journal transaction. On a disk a directory is a file of names, so [ext4_init_new_dir](ext4_init_new_dir) writes its first block with its own two entries, "." (itself) and ".." (its parent), and [ext4_add_entry](ext4_add_entry) puts the name "sub" into a block of /mnt, the parent.
2. Listing /mnt: [ext4_readdir](ext4_readdir) reads the directory's blocks and hands out one entry after another.
Try: [list the new directory instead](try:1): only "." and "..". Or make a file in it first, then list it.
title: A directory on a disk

name: link
text: A name is not the file. The file is its inode; a directory entry is a name that points to it, and an inode can have several.

1. [vfs_link](vfs_link), then ext4's [__ext4_link](__ext4_link): [inc_nlink](inc_nlink) counts the inode's names, from 1 to 2, and [__ext4_add_entry](__ext4_add_entry) writes "also.txt" into /mnt's directory block, with the same inode number; [d_instantiate](d_instantiate) points the new name's dentry at the same inode.

2. Removing the first name: [ext4_delete_entry](ext4_delete_entry) takes "note.txt" out of the directory, and [drop_nlink](drop_nlink) counts the names down, from 2 to 1: [what it changed](drop_nlink/memory). The inode stays: it still has a name. A file goes only when its last name does, as the next lesson shows.
Try: [read it by its new name](try:1): the same bytes, "hello from the disk".
title: A file with two names

name: remove
text: Names made, names taken away. Four calls on ext4: a name moves, a directory will not go while it has names in it, and a file goes when its last name does.
1. Renaming within one directory: [ext4_rename](ext4_rename) changes the entry's name from "a.txt" to "b.txt"; the inode stays as it is.
2. Removing the directory: [ext4_empty_dir](ext4_empty_dir) asks whether it is empty. It is not ("b.txt" is in it), so the call fails with ENOTEMPTY.

3. Removing the file: [ext4_delete_entry](unlinkat#2/ext4_delete_entry) takes the name out of the directory block, and since it was the file's only name and nobody has it open, [ext4_free_inode](ext4_free_inode) frees the inode.
4. Now the directory is empty: [ext4_free_blocks](unlinkat#3/ext4_free_blocks) gives its block back to the block bitmap, and its inode is freed too.
Try: [open b.txt before removing it](try:1): the name goes, but the inode stays until the close, which is where `ext4_free_inode` runs then. Or [rename across directories](try:2), to /mnt/b.txt.
title: Renaming and removing

name: sleep
text: So far every call ran straight through. Some wait: a sleep of 30 ms takes 30 ms, but the kernel works for only a tiny part of it. What happens in between?
1. [hrtimer_nanosleep](hrtimer_nanosleep) sets a high-resolution timer for 30 ms from now.

2. [schedule](schedule): nothing to do until then, so the CPU is given away. The idle task (swapper) runs and waits for an interrupt. The strip under the timeline shows which task ran when: the long stretch is idle.
3. 30 ms later the timer's interrupt fires and [hrtimer_wakeup](hrtimer_wakeup) makes the sleeper runnable again; the call returns 0.
Try: [sleep for 0 ns](try:1): does it still schedule? Or [CLOCK_REALTIME](try:2) instead of CLOCK_MONOTONIC.
title: Where does the time go when a program sleeps?

name: wait
program: void *mem = mmap2(NULL, 65536, PROT_READ | PROT_WRITE, MAP_PRIVATE | MAP_ANONYMOUS, -1, 0)
pid_t child = clone(CLONE_VM | SIGCHLD, mem + 65536, NULL, NULL, 0)
text: A parent waits for its child with a wait: `waitid` sleeps until the child has exited, then collects what it exited with.
1. [copy_process](copy_process) makes the child, a process of its own; SIGCHLD in the flags is the signal its parent is sent when it ends.
2. The wait: [do_wait](do_wait) finds the child still running, so the parent sleeps on its wait queue for children, `wait_chldexit`. The call blocks.

3. The child exits: [do_exit](do_exit) tears it down, and [exit_notify](exit_notify) tells the parent: it sends SIGCHLD and wakes the waiters ([__wake_up_parent](__wake_up_parent)). The child is a zombie now: gone, but for what it exited with.
4. Back in the parent: [wait_task_zombie](wait_task_zombie) collects the exit code, 3, into `info`, and frees what is left of the child ([release_task](release_task)). The wait returns 0.
Try: [the exit before the wait](try:1): the wait then finds a zombie at once, and returns without a sleep.
title: How does a parent wait for its child to end?
tries: void *mem = mmap2(NULL, 65536, PROT_READ | PROT_WRITE, MAP_PRIVATE | MAP_ANONYMOUS, -1, 0)

name: pipe
program: void *mem = mmap2(NULL, 65536, PROT_READ | PROT_WRITE, MAP_PRIVATE | MAP_ANONYMOUS, -1, 0)
pid_t child = clone(CLONE_VM | SIGCHLD, mem + 65536, NULL, NULL, 0)
text: Threads share memory; processes talk through the kernel. The program makes a pipe and starts a child that reads from it, as the `cat` in a shell's `echo hello | cat` would.
1. [create_pipe_files](create_pipe_files): a pipe is a buffer in the kernel and two files for it. The program's line shows the fds: 3 reads, 4 writes.

2. [copy_process](copy_process) makes the child, a process of its own (not CLONE_THREAD): with no MMU it shares the program's memory (CLONE_VM, on the stack `mem` gives it), but [dup_fd](dup_fd) gives it a copy of the program's fds, the pipe's too.
3. The child reads: [anon_pipe_read](anon_pipe_read) finds the pipe empty, so it sleeps. The read blocks: its line says it returned only during the program's write, the next line.

4. The program writes hello: [anon_pipe_write](anon_pipe_write) puts the bytes into the pipe's buffer, and [try_to_wake_up](try_to_wake_up) wakes the reader. The child's read returns the 6 bytes: see `buf`.

Try: [the end of input](try:1): once every writing end is closed, the child's own too, a read returns 0 (`pipe_release` wakes the readers); or [the child's end](try:2): it exits, and the parent, told by SIGCHLD, reaps it with waitid (`wait_task_zombie`, `release_task`).

name: kill
program: void *mem = mmap2(NULL, 65536, PROT_READ | PROT_WRITE, MAP_PRIVATE | MAP_ANONYMOUS, -1, 0)
pid_t child = clone(CLONE_VM | SIGCHLD, mem + 65536, NULL, NULL, 0)
text: Every wait so far ended when what it waited for came. A signal ends one too. The child reads a pipe nobody will write to; the program kills it.

1. [__send_signal_locked](kill/__send_signal_locked) marks SIGKILL pending for the child (signal 9: the bit that is 256 in its mask); [complete_signal](complete_signal) chooses the task to act on it, and [signal_wake_up](signal_wake_up) wakes it from its wait ([try_to_wake_up](try_to_wake_up)).

2. In the child: its wait gives up ([anon_pipe_read](anon_pipe_read) returns, a signal pending), and on its way back to its program [get_signal](get_signal) finds the signal. SIGKILL's action is to end the process: [do_group_exit](do_group_exit), [do_exit](do_exit), its exit code 9. Its line says it exited: its read never returns.
Try: [signal 0](try:1): `kill(child, 0)` only checks that the child is there, and sends nothing: the child stays blocked.

name: yours
text: You have seen the lessons; now make any syscall, with the arguments you give, written as in C.

Write, as in C: numbers (`0644`, `0x41`, `-100`); the kernel's constants (`O_CREAT | O_WRONLY`, `AT_FDCWD`); `"strings"`; structs, laid out as the parameter's type says (`{0, 30000000}`); results by name (`int fd = openat(…)`, then `fd`); and your program's own variables, declared as in C (`char buf[64]`, `int fds[2]`, `struct __kernel_timespec ts = {0, 30000000}`), for the kernel to fill or read: `read(fd, buf, 64)`, `&ts`, `fds[1]`.
